requests.text: In the stated tenant/trespasser setting, the Court held that the landlord retained legal or constructive possession through the tenant and could seek Section 6 recovery when that tenant was forcibly dispossessed by a third party. This resolves standing, not independently verified title or filing timeliness.

counterarguments: The contesting defendants argued that the house was joint-family property, that defendant no. 4 lacked authority to sell it, and that they themselves were co-owners in possession of the whole house. These are explicit opposing litigant positions at IK-161859415:L74. They must be preserved as opposition to the plaintiff's pleaded ownership and possession account, but the source does not establish them as findings that defeat the reported trial possession finding at IK-161859415:L76.

Defendant no. 4 separately alleged that no consideration was paid and that the sale deed was obtained by fraud, at IK-161859415:L74. This challenges the plaintiff's acquisition narrative but remains a pleaded objection. The Supreme Court characterized the trial court's title issue as unnecessary at IK-161859415:L75. Neither an authenticated transfer nor adjudicated fraud can be inferred.

The contesting defendants advanced a tenant-only Section 6 standing interpretation in revision, recorded at IK-161859415:L80. The High Court rejected that argument, and the Supreme Court's reasoning at IK-161859415:L151-L155 supports the landlord's competence to sue in the specified setting. The rejected objection remains valid evidence of the defendants' position, not a negative finding about the landlady's standing.

The Madras High Court's reported Veeraswami Mudali position restricted summary recovery where the landlord lacked the right to enjoy physical possession, at IK-161859415:L101. The Nagpur Judicial Commissioners' reported Ramchandra position denied standing because the landlord was neither in possession nor dispossessed, at IK-161859415:L103. These are important contrary interpretations, but the target Supreme Court expressly rejected them at IK-161859415:L156. Their underlying decisions have not been independently inspected.

The earlier Madras decision in (Kanneganti) Ramamanemma reportedly treated a landlord's Section 9 suit without the tenant's joinder as unmaintainable, at IK-161859415:L104. The Supreme Court expressly disagreed at IK-161859415:L156 and L159. This historical objection is relevant to the joinder question but cannot establish that Warik was actually omitted in the target proceedings.

The Bombay formulation quoted at IK-161859415:L114-L116 distinguished between proceedings in the tenant's name on a possessory right and proceedings in the landlord's own name for an injury to reversion. The target court approved the own-name principle at IK-161859415:L158. That approval does not independently prove a separately pleaded or established reversionary injury in this particular suit.

The supportive Calcutta precedent quoted at IK-161859415:L110-L112 involved tenants who relinquished the land to the plaintiff after dispossession. The Rajasthan precedent quoted at IK-161859415:L135-L139 discussed tenant participation and particular findings concerning collusion and a compromise decree. These circumstances belong to the reported historical cases and cannot be imported as facts concerning P.V. Warik.

Section 6(1) as quoted at IK-161859415:L84 requires dispossession without consent and otherwise than in due course of law. Section 6(2), quoted at IK-161859415:L86-L89, imposes a six-month filing restriction and excludes suits against the Government. The record supplies an alleged dispossession date and subsequent judicial dates but no independently established filing date or complete evidence addressing every statutory condition. The standing and joinder translations cannot be treated as full statutory compliance determinations.

The Supreme Court explained at IK-161859415:L157 that a dispossessed tenant may lack interest, be unavailable, or be unwilling to litigate. These are hypothetical explanations for declining to impose an absolute joinder requirement. Neither the abbreviated party description at IK-161859415:L71-L73 nor the doctrinal discussion at L157-L159 conclusively establishes whether Warik was joined, omitted, unavailable, unwilling, or uninterested.

The trial court's possession finding, reported at IK-161859415:L76, concerns possession through a tenant. Treating it as proof of the plaintiff's own physical occupation would contradict the Supreme Court's express distinction between actual and legal possession at IK-161859415:L151-L154. Similarly, using the target standing conclusion P13 to establish the earlier trial finding P6 would reverse the evidentiary and reasoning relationship.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal at IK-161859415:L160. That disposition must remain outside the evidentiary basis for reconstructing the earlier findings and legal evaluations. A successful outcome does not independently validate ownership, tenancy documents, the underlying evidence, actual nonjoinder or every statutory prerequisite.

all_raw_relations.reason: The defendants disputed the authority for the alleged sale and asserted their own title; neither side's claim is treated as proved.
The purported seller challenged consideration and alleged fraud concerning the same pleaded 1981 transfer.
The pleaded letting supplies the plaintiff's tenancy narrative; the trial court separately treated her as possessing through a tenant.
The pleaded October 1988 takeover and trial-court finding concern the same alleged dispossession, but the pleading is not independent proof.
The defendants' claimed possession and co-ownership conflict with the trial finding of dispossession through the tenant; title is a separate issue.
The tenant-only objection was expressly rejected in revision.
The tenant-only interpretation conflicts with the target court's legal-possession account of standing.
The matched recorded trial possession finding supplies the factual attribution needed for standing in this case.
The High Court's reported standing interpretation accords with the Supreme Court's reasoning, without substituting for it.
The statutory claiming-through formulation provides the identified Section 6 procedural route.
Retained legal possession explains why removal of the physical tenant is attributed to the landlord.
Legal possession through a tenant supports the landlady's standing notwithstanding lack of personal physical occupation.
The deemed landlord dispossession links the found tenant-dispossession setting to Section 6 standing.
The historical Madras view made the landlord's own physical possessory entitlement central; the Supreme Court rejected it.
The historical Nagpur view denied qualifying dispossession to the landlord; the Supreme Court rejected it.
The Bombay reversion analysis supplies supportive historical reasoning for an action in the landlord's own name.
The trial finding places the case within the landlord/tenant/third-party-dispossession setting of the joinder discussion.
The landlord's recognized ability to sue independently of the tenant underpins the non-absolute joinder approach.
Section 6 permits a person claiming through the dispossessed person to bring the suit, undermining an absolute tenant-party requirement.
The Supreme Court approvingly referred to the Bombay view permitting the landlord to sue in the landlord's own name.
The historical Madras nonjoinder rule is contrary to the target court's express holding.
Possible nonparticipation by the tenant supports refusal to impose an absolute joinder requirement; no case-specific reason is proved.
The text does not establish the actual tenant-party status, which cannot be inferred from the general rule on nonjoinder.
The target court treated a title issue as unnecessary rather than deciding the co-ownership assertion in this summary proceeding.
